evidence.summary: Several small clinical trials show Arjuna improves left ventricular ejection fraction, reduces angina frequency, and lowers blood pressure in stable coronary artery disease and heart failure. Mechanistic studies show antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and inotropic effects.

evidence.summary: Clinical trials show guggulsterones reduce total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides in hyperlipidemia. Some studies report modest HDL increase. Effects are generally modest compared to statins. Safety profile favorable in short-term studies.

data.preparationAndDose: Neem leaf decoction 50-100 ml + Guduchi stem decoction 50-100 ml twice daily, or as directed by an Ayurvedic practitioner. Not a substitute for antibiotics in serious infections.

evidence.summary: Neem shows broad-spectrum antibacterial activity in vitro against S. aureus, E. coli, P. aeruginosa. Guduchi demonstrates immunomodulatory and antimicrobial effects in animal models. Limited human clinical trial data for acute bacterial infections.

citations.ref: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 1 (Nimba pp. 156-160), Vol. 3 (Guduchi pp. 88-92)

interactionNotes: Neem may have mild hypoglycemic effect - monitor with diabetes meds
Guduchi generally well-tolerated

data.preparationAndDose: Boswellia standardized extract 300-500 mg (65% boswellic acids) 2-3 times daily with meals + Guggul 500 mg twice daily, or as directed by an Ayurvedic practitioner.

evidence.summary: Multiple RCTs show Boswellia serrata extract significantly reduces pain and improves function in osteoarthritis of the knee. Guggul has anti-inflammatory effects. Combination used traditionally. Effects are generally slower onset than NSAIDs.

citations.ref: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 3 (Shallaki pp. 12-16), Vol. 2 (Guggulu pp. 88-93)

formulation.nameCommon: Glycyrrhiza glabra (Yashtimadhu) root + Phyllanthus emblica (Amalaki) fruit
formulation.classicalSource: Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana 15 (Amlapitta Chikitsa); Ashtanga Hridaya, Chikitsa Sthana 8
formulation.pharmacopoeiaRef: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 1 (Yashtimadhu), Vol. 2 (Amalaki)

ingredients.dose: 1-3 g powder or 250-500 mg DGL (deglycyrrhizinated) extract

data.traditionalUse: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for Amlapitta (hyperacidity/GERD), Parinama Shoola (duodenal ulcer), and as a Rasayana for gastric mucosa protection and healing.
data.preparationAndDose: Yashtimadhu (preferably DGL) 250-500 mg + Amalaki 500-1000 mg twice daily before meals, or as directed by an Ayurvedic practitioner. DGL preferred for long-term use to avoid glycyrrhizin side effects.

evidence.summary: DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) shows efficacy in peptic ulcer healing comparable to antacids/H2 blockers in older trials. Amalaki demonstrates gastroprotective, antioxidant, and H. pylori inhibitory effects in preclinical studies. Human data limited but supportive.

citations.ref: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 1 (Yashtimadhu pp. 212-216), Vol. 2 (Amalaki pp. 12-16)

interactionNotes: Regular licorice (glycyrrhizin) causes pseudohyperaldosteronism: hypertension, hypokalemia, edema - USE DGL
DGL avoids mineralocorticoid effects
Amalaki may enhance iron absorption

Do not stop or change prescribed acid-reducing medications without consulting your healthcare provider. Use deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) for safety.

evidence.summary: Arjuna has clinical evidence for heart failure/angina (see ay_lisinopril_001). Pushkarmool shows vasodilatory and inotropic effects in preclinical studies. Limited human trial data for Pushkarmool specifically. Classical texts describe combination for cardiac disorders.

evidence.summary: Punarnava shows diuretic activity in animal models (increased urine output, Na+/K+ excretion). Gokshura demonstrates mild diuretic and nephroprotective effects in preclinical studies. Limited human clinical trial data for edema/hypertension.

citations.ref: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 2 (Punarnava pp. 132-136), Vol. 3 (Gokshura pp. 112-116)

data.preparationAndDose: As directed by an Ayurvedic practitioner. Typically combined formulation. Vijaysar wood tumbler water (overnight soak) consumed morning. NOT a substitute for insulin.

evidence.summary: Vijaysar (Pterocarpus marsupium) shows beta-cell regenerative and insulin-sensitizing effects in animal models; pterostilbene identified as active compound. Gymnema reduces glucose absorption. Jamun seed shows antihyperglycemic effects. Human data limited to small open-label studies.

citations.ref: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 3 (Gudmar pp. 77-81), Vol. 2 (Vijaysar pp. 144-148, Jamun pp. 108-112)

Requires EXTREME CAUTION and frequent glucose monitoring
Insulin dose reduction may be needed under strict medical supervision
contraindications: Type 1 diabetes (insulin-dependent) - NOT a substitute for insulin

formulation.nameCommon: CONTRAINDICATED - No safe Ayurvedic parallel for anticoagulation
formulation.classicalSource: None - Ayurveda does not have a classical anticoagulant equivalent

data.traditionalUse: Ayurveda does not have a traditional anticoagulant equivalent for mechanical valve stroke prevention or atrial fibrillation thromboembolism prophylaxis. Herbs with antiplatelet effects (e.g., garlic, ginger, turmeric) are NOT substitutes and INCREASE bleeding risk with warfarin.
data.preparationAndDose: NOT APPLICABLE. Do not use Ayurvedic herbs as anticoagulant substitutes.

evidence.summary: No Ayurvedic formulation has demonstrated efficacy comparable to warfarin for stroke prevention in AF or mechanical valve thrombosis prophylaxis. Herbs like garlic, ginger, turmeric, ginkgo have antiplatelet effects that ADD to warfarin bleeding risk. This entry exists to explicitly warn against substitution attempts.

interactionNotes: ABSOLUTELY DO NOT COMBINE antiplatelet herbs (garlic, ginger, turmeric, ginkgo, ginseng) with warfarin
Dramatically increased bleeding risk
Many Ayurvedic formulations contain these herbs
contraindications: Any herb with unknown coagulation effects

data.disclaimer: CRITICAL WARNING: Warfarin has a NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX. NO Ayurvedic herb or formulation is a safe substitute for warfarin in stroke prevention or mechanical valve prophylaxis. Herbs with antiplatelet effects (garlic, ginger, turmeric, ginkgo, ginseng, etc.) DANGEROUSLY INCREASE bleeding risk when combined with warfarin. This entry exists to PREVENT harm. Do not seek Ayurvedic alternatives for anticoagulation. Consult your cardiologist/hematologist for any medication changes.

data.traditionalUse: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for Pratishyaya (allergic rhinitis), Kasa (cough), and Sheetapitta (urticaria/allergic skin reactions), modulating immune response and reducing histamine-mediated symptoms.
data.preparationAndDose: Haridra 1-3 g + Tulsi leaf juice 5-10 ml + Shirish bark decoction 50-100 ml twice daily, or as directed by an Ayurvedic practitioner.

evidence.summary: Curcumin inhibits histamine release from mast cells in vitro. Tulsi shows antiallergic and immunomodulatory effects in animal models. Shirish (Albizia lebbeck) demonstrated antihistaminic and mast cell stabilizing effects in preclinical studies. Human clinical trials limited.

citations.ref: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 2 (Haridra pp. 52-56), Vol. 1 (Tulsi pp. 208-212), Vol. 3 (Shirish pp. 18-22)

formulation.pharmacopoeiaRef: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 1 (Vasa), Vol. 2 (Kantakari), Vol. 3 (Pushkarmool)

data.traditionalUse: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for Shwasa (bronchial asthma/dyspnea), Kasa (cough), and Hikka (hiccups), acting as bronchodilators, expectorants, and anti-inflammatory agents for respiratory passages.
data.preparationAndDose: Vasa leaf decoction 50-100 ml + Kantakari decoction 50-100 ml + Pushkarmool root decoction 50 ml 2-3 times daily, or as directed by an Ayurvedic practitioner. NOT a substitute for rescue inhaler in acute bronchospasm.

evidence.summary: Vasica (vasicine) shows bronchodilatory and expectorant effects in preclinical studies; semi-synthetic derivatives (bromhexine) used as mucolytics. Kantakari demonstrates bronchodilatory and antihistaminic effects in animal models. Pushkarmool shows vasodilatory effects. No human trials for acute bronchospasm.

citations.ref: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 1 (Vasa pp. 220-224), Vol. 2 (Kantakari pp. 60-64), Vol. 3 (Pushkarmool pp. 102-106)

NOT a replacement for SABA in acute bronchospasm

formulation.nameCommon: Terminalia arjuna (Arjuna) bark + Rauwolfia serpentina (Sarpagandha) root
formulation.classicalSource: Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana 26 (Hridroga); Sarpagandha described in later texts (Bhavaprakasha, 16th century)
formulation.pharmacopoeiaRef: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 1 (Arjuna), Vol. 3 (Sarpagandha)

ingredients.dose: 50-100 mg standardized extract (reserpine content) - UNDER MEDICAL SUPERVISION ONLY

data.traditionalUse: Traditionally used in Ayurveda for Hridroga (heart diseases) and Uccha Raktachapa (hypertension). Sarpagandha (reserpine) was the first effective antihypertensive in modern medicine (1950s), derived from this plant.
data.preparationAndDose: Arjuna bark decoction 50-100 ml twice daily. Sarpagandha ONLY under strict medical supervision due to narrow therapeutic index and psychiatric side effects. NOT for self-medication.

evidence.summary: Reserpine (from Sarpagandha) is a PROVEN antihypertensive with historical significance - first effective oral antihypertensive. Depletes catecholamines. However, significant side effects (depression, parkinsonism, GI) limit modern use. Arjuna has clinical evidence for cardiac benefit (see ay_lisinopril_001). Combination used traditionally.

citations.ref: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Vol. 1 (Arjuna pp. 44-48), Vol. 3 (Sarpagandha pp. 120-124)

interactionNotes: Sarpagandha (reserpine) + calcium channel blockers: additive hypotension, bradycardia, depression risk
Reserpine has NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX - depression, suicide risk, parkinsonism
REQUIRES strict medical supervision
Many drug interactions (MAOIs, antidepressants, etc.)

data.disclaimer: CRITICAL: Sarpagandha contains reserpine - a potent drug with NARROW THERAPEUTIC INDEX and serious side effects (depression, parkinsonism). This entry is for HISTORICAL/INFORMATIONAL purposes ONLY. Do NOT self-medicate with Sarpagandha. It requires STRICT MEDICAL SUPERVISION. Do not stop or change prescribed calcium channel blockers without consulting your cardiologist.
